blocks.text: 翻译一个网站并让译文保持最新并不容易，对我们来说尤其如此。OpenRouter 的站点有 16,918 条英文字符串，而且我们每天都在改动其中一些，所以一次性的翻译一周之内就会过时。我们搭建了一套循环流程来大规模处理这件事。它每天找出发生变动的字符串，翻译它们，在代码中提交，再由第二个模型对照英文核验含义。当某条译文未通过检查，或核验模型将其驳回时，循环会把原因一并附上退回重试。这个重试循环正是系统自我纠错的部分。

blocks.text: 仍有一些错误会漏过去，由人来发现。当审校人员和读者报告错误时，我们会把它转成一条术语表规则、一条风格说明或一条覆盖规则；而每日审校发现的错误也会变成测试用例，未来每个模型都必须通过。整条流水线都运行在 OpenRouter 上。

blocks.text: 在任何模型介入之前，译文需要有个落脚之处。我们用开源的 General Translation 运行时在 React 代码中包裹字符串。译文以 JSON 目录的形式与代码一起提交，运行时在本地加载，因此请求路径上不经过任何翻译服务。字符串合并后一天之内就会被纳入翻译。在此之前，页面显示英文原文。每条译文条目还会存下其英文来源的指纹。一旦有人修改了英文，指纹就不再匹配，该条目会被重新放回队列。这条规则让每日运行能找出所有过时条目，而无需重新翻译整个目录。

blocks.text: 脚本扫描前端，把每个被包裹的英文字符串写入源目录。每条条目记录其所在文件和 UI 角色，例如按钮、标题或表头。角色很重要，因为同一个英文单词在不同位置可能需要不同的译法。按钮上的“Queue”是一条指令，而本文后面提到的一个缺陷，就是模型把它译成了名词。

blocks.text: 3. 检查

inlines.text: 3. 检查

blocks.text: 代码会拒绝以下回复：破坏 ICU 占位符、复数分支、富文本标签，或首尾空白，或以术语表禁止的形式呈现产品术语。我们会把被拒的批次拆小后重发，并说明失败原因，默认最多重试 4 轮。上限是一个可调设置，最高可到 20。经过最后一轮仍然失败的字符串保留英文，并在拉取请求中标记出来。

blocks.text: 4. 校验

inlines.text: 4. 校验

blocks.text: 第二次调用同一个模型，让它充当校验者，对照英文逐条阅读译文，并按严重程度列出错误。任何严重或重大错误，比如漏译从句、意思颠倒，都会把该字符串退回给翻译器，并附上此前所有异议。翻译器在首次尝试之后最多可重试 3 次，最后一次重试会投入更多推理。每个字符串的花费没有单独上限，因为重试次数本身已经限定了开销。算上校验重发，一个字符串最多可经历四次翻译尝试，每次最多四轮校验，外加每次尝试后的一次校验调用。这样最坏情况下，每个字符串每种语言约需 20 次模型调用。如果校验器宕机，流水线不写入任何内容，字符串保留英文。读者看到一天英文，也好过看到未经校验的译文。

blocks.text: 在验证器出现之前，我们用一个独立的评判模型给每一条译文打分，凡是被它标记或判定为不确定的，都会重新翻译。为了检验效果，我们给一个基准集标注了三类字符串：已知错误、修正后的译文（对早前错误手工修复的版本，理应通过），以及一份干净样本。评判模型确实抓到了真问题。在一次基准运行中，它把该次运行中 91% 的真实缺陷标记为不确定。但它也误报了 14 条修正译文中的 11 条、150 条干净样本中的 42 条，导致大量本来合格的译文被退回重译。

blocks.text: 起初，验证器每次重试都拒绝的字符串会一直保持未翻译状态，直到有人手工修复。对整个目录做一次完整重译——16,274 条字符串译成 7 种语言——留下了 97 条这样的字符串（0.09%）。现在流水线会按验证器发现的问题给被拒的草稿排序，提交其中错误最少的一版，并在拉取请求中标记出来供审查。这个循环最终总会产出一条译文，即使这条译文仍带有被标记的错误，而标记会让它直接呈现在合并拉取请求的人面前。

blocks.text: 验证器的首轮数据基数不同。裸模型用的是通过代码检查的 306 条字符串，流水线用的是全部 454 条。验证器与译者来自同一模型家族，所以它的通过率只能说明模型在多大程度上与自己一致。两项工作我们都用 GPT-6.1 Sol，因为在我们测试的两个译者中它更准确。为了获得外部视角，评测还会把每一对译文匿名送给来自其他模型家族的三个评判模型：Claude Opus 5.5、Gemini 4 Argon 和 DeepSeek V4 Pro。三个评判模型合计在流水线输出中发现 109 个严重错误，在裸模型输出中发现 203 个。每个评判模型发现的错误单独计数，所以三个评判模型都标记的字符串会在总数中计三次。

blocks.text: Translating a website and keeping that translation up-to-date is hard, especially true for us. OpenRouter’s site has 16,918 English strings, and we change some of them every day, so a one-time translation would be out of date within a week. We built a loop to help us do this at scale. Every day, it finds the strings that changed, translates them, checks them in code, and has a second model verify the meaning against the English. When a translation fails a check, or the verifier rejects it, the loop sends it back with the reason attached and tries again. That retry loop is the part of the system that corrects itself.

Every day, it finds the strings that changed, translates them, checks them in code, and has a second model verify the meaning against the English. When a translation fails a check, or the verifier rejects it, the loop sends it back with the reason attached and tries again. That retry loop is the part of the system that corrects itself.

blocks.text: Some mistakes still get past it, and people catch those. When reviewers and readers report a mistake, we turn it into a glossary rule, a style note, or an override, and mistakes the daily review catches also become test cases that every future model has to pass. The whole pipeline runs on OpenRouter.

blocks.text: Translations live in Git next to the code

inlines.text: Translations live in Git next to the code

blocks.text: Before any model gets involved, the translations need a home. We use the open-source General Translation runtime to wrap strings in our React code. We commit translations as JSON catalogs next to the code and load them locally at runtime, so no translation service sits in the request path. A string gets picked up for translation within a day of it merging. Until then, the page shows the English source. Each translated entry also stores a fingerprint of the English it came from. When someone edits the English, the fingerprint stops matching, and the entry goes back in the queue. This rule lets the daily run find every stale entry without retranslating the whole catalog.

blocks.text: The pipeline

inlines.text: The pipeline

blocks.text: Every string in that queue goes through five stages before it reaches the site.

inlines.text: Every string in that queue goes through five stages before it reaches the site.

blocks.alt: How a string gets translated: new text goes to a translator model, then code checks, then a verifier model, then review, then live. Failed checks and verifier rejections go back to the translator, and fixes flagged by reviewers or readers go into the glossary.

blocks.text: A script scans the frontend and writes every wrapped English string to a source catalog. Each entry records its file and its UI role, such as button, heading, or table header. The role matters because the same English word can need a different translation in a different place. “Queue” on a button is an instruction, and one of the defects later in this post is a model translating it as a noun.

blocks.text: 2. Translate

inlines.text: 2. Translate

blocks.text: We send new and changed strings to GPT-6.1 Sol in batches of up to 40, and use Structured Outputs to hold the reply to a strict JSON schema. Each request carries our global and per-language style notes, the glossary rules for any product term in the batch, and the UI role of each string.

blocks.text: Because every model on OpenRouter takes the same request, trying a different translator means changing only the model slug. That is how we ran the model comparison later in this post.

blocks.text: 3. Check

inlines.text: 3. Check

blocks.text: Code rejects a reply that breaks an ICU placeholder, a plural branch, a rich-text tag, or leading or trailing whitespace, or that renders a product term in a form the glossary forbids. We resend a rejected batch in smaller pieces, naming the failure, for up to 4 passes by default. The limit is a setting that goes up to 20. A string that still fails after the last pass stays in English and is flagged in the pull request.

We resend a rejected batch in smaller pieces, naming the failure, for up to 4 passes by default. The limit is a setting that goes up to 20. A string that still fails after the last pass stays in English and is flagged in the pull request.

blocks.text: 4. Verify

inlines.text: 4. Verify

blocks.text: A second call to the same model, acting as verifier, reads each translation against the English and lists errors by severity. Any critical or major error, such as a dropped clause or a reversed meaning, sends the string back to the translator with every objection so far attached. The translator gets up to 3 retries after its first attempt, and the last retry uses more reasoning effort. Spend per string has no separate cap, because the retry limits already bound it. Counting the check resends, a string can take up to four translation attempts with up to four check passes each, plus a verifier call after each attempt. That puts the worst case at about 20 model calls per string per language. If the verifier is down, the pipeline writes nothing and the string stays in English. A reader who sees English for a day is better off than one who sees an unchecked translation.

Counting the check resends, a string can take up to four translation attempts with up to four check passes each, plus a verifier call after each attempt. That puts the worst case at about 20 model calls per string per language. If the verifier is down, the pipeline writes nothing and the string stays in English. A reader who sees English for a day is better off than one who sees an unchecked translation.

blocks.text: A cheaper translator

inlines.text: A cheaper translator

blocks.text: We first tested a smaller, cheaper model, GPT-6 Luna (openai/gpt-6-luna). In the model comparison, it passed 91.7% of cases on the first try, against 99.2% for GPT-6.1 Sol. Its weakest languages were Korean and Japanese. Its hardest failures were replies that General Translation, our translation framework, couldn’t compile, such as its translation of “Legacy alias of {value}”. Those failures persisted through every retry.

blocks.text: A separate judge model

inlines.text: A separate judge model

blocks.text: Before the verifier existed, a separate judge model scored every translation, and we retranslated anything it flagged or marked uncertain. To see how well it worked, we labeled a benchmark with three kinds of strings: known errors, corrected translations (hand-fixed versions of earlier errors, which should pass), and a clean sample. The judge did catch real problems. In one benchmark run, it marked 91% of that run’s real defects as uncertain. It also flagged 11 of the 14 corrected translations and 42 of the 150 clean ones, so it sent a lot of good work back for retranslation.

blocks.text: With the verifier in place, turning the judge off lowered first-pass accuracy from 99.2% to 98.8% and left the final result unchanged. The judge had been sending about 45% of first drafts back for retranslation. We now leave it off by default.

blocks.text: Leaving hard strings for a person

inlines.text: Leaving hard strings for a person

blocks.text: At first, a string the verifier rejected on every retry stayed untranslated until someone fixed it by hand. A full retranslation of the catalog, 16,274 strings into 7 languages, left 97 such strings (0.09%). Now the pipeline ranks the rejected drafts by the verifier’s findings, commits the least-wrong one, and flags it in the pull request for review. The loop always ends in a translation, even when that translation still carries a flagged error, and the flag puts it in front of the person who merges the pull request.

blocks.text: The verifier’s first-pass figures use different bases. For the bare model it’s the 306 strings that passed the code checks, and for the pipeline it’s all 454. The verifier comes from the same model family as the translator, so its pass rate tells us how often the model agrees with itself. We use GPT-6.1 Sol for both jobs because it was the more accurate of the two translators we tested. For an outside view, the eval also sends each pair of translations, unlabeled, to three judges from other model families, Claude Opus 5.5, Gemini 4 Argon, and DeepSeek V4 Pro. Across the three judges, they found 109 critical errors in the pipeline’s output and 203 in the bare model’s. Each judge’s errors count separately, so a string that all three judges flag adds three to the total.

inlines.text: The feedback loop

blocks.text: The verifier catches most errors before they ship, and readers catch some of the rest.

inlines.text: The verifier catches most errors before they ship, and readers catch some of the rest.

blocks.text: Turn on select-to-report in the Language dialog, then highlight any translated text, add a note, and send it. Each report arrives with the language, the page, and the exact text. A model triages it first, picks one of four fixes, and puts the fix up within minutes. Our AI reviewer checks the fix, and a person does the final merge.

inlines.text: Turn on select-to-report in the Language dialog, then highlight any translated text, add a note, and send it. Each report arrives with the language, the page, and the exact text. A model triages it first, picks one of four fixes, and puts the fix up within minutes. Our AI reviewer checks the fix, and a person does the final merge.
Wrong meaning.
The string reverts to English the same day, then gets a corrected translation.
Wrong term.

We add the term to the glossary with the accepted form and the forms to reject for that language. We pin compliance and protocol names such as HIPAA, SOC 2, OAuth, and SAML so the pipeline leaves them in English.
Wrong tone or punctuation.
The rule goes into that language’s style notes.
One bad string.
An exact override pins the approved wording, and no later run can change it.

blocks.text: Mistakes the daily review catches after the verifier passed them go into the defects suite. It has 22 cases so far. They include “Queue” translated as a noun on a button that needed a verb, “shadow traffic” rendered as road traffic, and a HIPAA setting whose meaning was inverted. Each case forbids the mistake that shipped, so any future model, prompt, or glossary change that brings it back fails the eval.

blocks.text: What it costs

inlines.text: What it costs

blocks.text: When we first priced it, a full retranslation of all 16,274 strings into 7 languages, 113,918 translations in total, came to about $430 with translation and verification included. We arrived at that figure by pricing production-sized batches in each language and scaling up. It works out to under half a cent per string per language. Verification is slightly more than half, about $228, or $0.002 per string per language. The catalog has since grown to 16,918 strings, and a full retranslation of it today costs about $460. The daily loop only sends what changed, and a day with 677 changed strings across 7 languages costs roughly $18.

blocks.text: What you can reuse

inlines.text: What you can reuse

blocks.text: If you are localizing your own product, four parts of this design carry over directly.

inlines.text: If you are localizing your own product, four parts of this design carry over directly.
Fingerprint every translation against its English source, so stale entries requeue themselves.
Let code reject broken placeholders, plural branches, tags, and forbidden terms before any model reviews the meaning.
Use a verifier that names each error and its severity, and send those objections back to the translator.
Turn every mistake a person catches into a glossary rule, a style note, an override, or an eval case.
